source: Jones & Steinhardt (2022) Capturing Failures of Large Language Models via Human Cognitive Biases
finding: GPT-3 (davinci-002) was given the Asian disease problem at many population sizes and save fractions. At the original save probability (1/3) it picked the risky option rarely under save wording and more under die wording, like humans.
numbers: Risky option chosen, mean over probabilities: save frame 45.4% (11.3% below p=0.5, 21.9% at 0.5, 84.4% above); die frame 74.1% (60.0%, 46.9%, 93.8%). Human original: 28% save, 78% die.
limits: At high save probability both frames pick the risky option, so the effect shrinks or vanishes. Base model, bare prompt, no CoT.
agent_relevance: Framing is real in raw LMs but depends on the numbers. Test the neutral restatement across a range of parameters, not one item.

source: Jones & Steinhardt (2022) Capturing Failures of Large Language Models via Human Cognitive Biases
finding: Related test in the same paper: irrelevant preceding code functions and a 'framing line' pushed Codex and CodeGen to copy the line, which cut accuracy. Framing here means prompt context, not gain/loss wording.
numbers: Codex HumanEval functional accuracy 32.9% original; 2.4% to 10.6% with a framing line plus irrelevant functions. Framing line copied verbatim in 62% to 93% of outputs (Codex).
limits: Different meaning of framing (context contamination). CodeGen drops from 25.6% to between 1.5% and 11.0%.
agent_relevance: Irrelevant or leading text in the prompt is copied. Restating the task in neutral terms and dropping noise matters for code steps too.

source: Suri, Slater, Ziaee, Nguyen (2023) Do Large Language Models Show Decision Heuristics Similar to Humans? A Case Study Using GPT-3.5
finding: ChatGPT showed a gain/loss framing effect on a medicine-efficacy rating, same direction as 82 MTurk humans. It rated the identical drug higher when told '70 improved' than '30 did not improve'.
numbers: ChatGPT: 5 in all 11 gain-frame trials, 4 in all 11 loss-frame trials (1-7 scale). Humans: 5.2 gain (n=44) vs 4.6 loss (n=39), t(80)=3.86, p<0.001.
quote: In all 11 trials in the positive frame, ChatGPT rated the efficacy of the medicine to be 5
limits: Rating task, not a choice. Zero variance in ChatGPT across 11 trials. Authors avoided the Asian disease wording.
agent_relevance: A 1-point shift from a pure restatement, with no spread across samples, shows resampling cannot detect frame bias. Neutral restatement should be done once, in code, before the model sees the numbers.

source: Suri et al. (2023) Do LLMs Show Decision Heuristics Similar to Humans?
finding: The same paper argues a model cannot feel loss aversion, so framing in LLMs is likely driven by language patterns and associations (for example 'did not improve' reads as negative).
numbers: Study 3 of 4 (with anchoring, representativeness, endowment). No mechanism test was run.
limits: Interpretation only; the competing explanation is learned text statistics.
agent_relevance: Supports treating frame effects as wording-to-association effects that a rewrite can remove, unlike human loss aversion.

source: Binz & Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3 (PNAS)
finding: GPT-3 showed the certainty effect and framing effect in decisions from descriptions, plus overweighting. It did not show reflection, isolation or magnitude-perception effects. Small wording changes to vignettes sent it far off.
numbers: Vignettes: 6 of 12 correct, all human-like. Decisions from descriptions: over 13,000 problems; davinci beat chance (t(29134)=-16.85) but stayed below humans (t=-11.50). 12 prompt variants on 2,500 gambles: 10 beat chance; question-style beat request-style (beta=0.19, p<.001).
quote: small perturbations to vignettes can lead GPT-3 vastly astray
limits: Fragility examples: Wason card order change; CRT bat worded 'costs $1.00 more than the bat' still answered $0.10. Asian disease not tested. GPT-3 only.
agent_relevance: Prompt style alone moves performance; paraphrase stability needs testing as a property of the whole pipeline.

source: Macmillan-Scott & Musolesi (2024) (Ir)rationality and cognitive biases in large language models
finding: Seven LLMs on 12 classic reasoning tasks. Most errors were not human-like, and answers varied across 10 repeats of the same prompt. No framing task and no rewording condition.
numbers: Correct and logical: GPT-4 69.2%, Claude 2 55.0%, Bard 35.8%, GPT-3.5 29.2%, Llama2-70b 15.0%. Incorrect human-like: GPT-3.5 21.7%, GPT-4 4.2%.
limits: Facilitated versions helped only on the AIDS task. Not a framing study; a boundary: LLM errors are not simply human bias.
agent_relevance: Do not assume LLM frame errors mirror humans. Measure the agent's own flip rate; do not import human debiasing blindly.

source: Echterhoff, Liu, Alessa, McAuley, He (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs
finding: Admissions question asked in admit-framed vs reject-framed wording. The admit-rate gap (admit minus reject) was large in GPT-3.5 and reversed sign in GPT-4. Awareness, counterfactual and contrastive prompts helped some models and hurt others.
numbers: GPT-3.5 gap +0.165 baseline, awareness +0.035, counterfactual +0.030. GPT-4 baseline -0.405, awareness -0.470, counterfactual -0.570. Llama-2-13b baseline -0.060, contrastive -0.568.
limits: Few-shot mitigations caused instruction failures in Llama-2-7b (admit near 0 or near 1). Single task.
agent_relevance: A generic 'be unbiased' instruction is not reliable. A wording flip can go in either direction, so test both frames and compare in code.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs
finding: The 'selfhelp' method, where the model rewrites its own prompt to remove bias-inducing wording, gave the smallest framing gap for GPT-4. This is a self-run restatement step, close to our S1.
numbers: GPT-4 gap -0.405 baseline to -0.010 with selfhelp. GPT-3.5 gap +0.165 to -0.080. Bias-inducing prompt elements cut to 2.7% (GPT-4).
limits: Self-rewrite made GPT-3.5 overshoot to the opposite sign. Admit and reject rates themselves fell for GPT-4 (0.27 and 0.28).
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that a neutral restatement step can erase a framing gap in a strong model. Check that the base rate is not distorted.

source: Itzhak, Stanovsky, Rosenfeld, Belinkov (2024) Instructed to Bias
finding: Instruction-tuned models showed stronger decoy, certainty and belief-bias effects than their base versions (Flan-T5 vs T5, Mistral-Instruct vs Mistral, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4).
numbers: Bias score is bounded; the paper gives per-model tables. Certainty effect uses sure amounts versus risky prizes with the same expected value.
limits: Certainty effect is a neighbor of framing, not framing. Cannot separate RLHF from instruction data. Only the abstract page and part of the text were read.
agent_relevance: Preference-construction effects are not removed by alignment training and may grow. The scaffold has to handle them.

source: Lore & Heydari (2024) Strategic behavior of LLMs: game structure versus contextual framing (Sci Rep)
finding: Same game payoffs were told in five stories. GPT-3.5 let the story decide more than the payoff; GPT-4 weighted the game structure more; Llama-2 was in between and swayed by the 'friends' context.
numbers: 4 games x 5 contexts x 300 runs per model; temperature 0.8. GPT-4 almost fully bimodal (all cooperate or all defect). Dominance ranking: GPT-3.5 contexts first, GPT-4 games first.
limits: Exact dominance values only in figures. GPT-4 still pulled to cooperation with a friend story.
agent_relevance: Stronger model, less story-driven, not zero. Supports stripping the story down to payoffs before choosing.

source: Wang & Zhang (2026) Framing Effects in Independent-Agent LLMs
finding: 82 models in 11 families picked option B 4.3% of the time under an 'instrumental' prompt and 68.8% under a 'cooperative' prompt of the same threshold game.
numbers: Scenario A: 1,472 A, 70 B, 98 non-compliant of 1,640. Scenario B: 346 A, 1,128 B, 166 non-compliant of 1,640. Gap 64.5 points. 20 trials per model per prompt, T=0.1. DeepSeek smallest shift; Mistral, Llama, Kimi near-total reversal.
limits: The two texts differ in more than frame (one states only your own survival rule, the other states the majority rule), so wording and information are confounded. Preprint, observational.
agent_relevance: Shows how large wording-only shifts can be across vendors. For us it is a warning that restated problems must keep all rules, not drop some.

source: Payne (2025) An analysis of AI decision under risk: prospect theory in LLMs
finding: Five LLMs (GPT-4o, o3, Claude Sonnet 4 with and without thinking, Gemini 1.5 Pro) got three equal-expected-value options in a loss frame ('trailing') or gain frame ('tied'). The effect appeared in some scenarios, reversed in one, and vanished with abstract math.
numbers: Championship: loss frame 85.6% chose risky BLITZ; gain frame 88.8% chose safe CONTROL. Career: reverse effect, loss frame 87.2% safe. Business merger: minimal. 25 runs per condition; about 2.3% unparsed. Abstract math: no effect, models declared indifference or chose the sure option.
limits: Counts in the paper do not add up (2,550 stated vs 2,150 in the table). Frames differ in context text beyond the number.
agent_relevance: With the numbers explicit and no story, frame effects disappeared. Strong support for a normalising step that computes expected values in code.

source: Payne (2025) An analysis of AI decision under risk
finding: Geopolitical scenarios mostly gave the classic effect, weaker for the trade route. The high-risk ESCALATE option was almost never chosen. A French version of the border dispute was also tested.
numbers: ESCALATE chosen in 1 of over 700 valid English decisions in the trade-route scenario.
limits: Safety training may floor risk-seeking in military contexts, hiding frame effects.
agent_relevance: Floor and ceiling effects can make a stable-looking answer unreliable. Probe with the frame flipped.

source: Shaikh, Dandekar, Panat, Dandekar (2024) CBEval: evaluating and interpreting cognitive biases in LLMs
finding: A stock choice flipped from B to A when '70% profit' was rewritten as '30% loss' on GPT-4o. Word-level Shapley scores showed 'loss' had the largest negative pull.
numbers: P(stock B): 0.9744 positive frame; 0.0868 negative frame (GPT-4o). GPT-4o-mini kept a preference for B until loss rates near 20% (a 'cognitive bias barrier').
limits: Single prompt pair, token probabilities, no human comparison. Also found round-number peaks at multiples of 10.
agent_relevance: A frame effect traced to single tokens is the kind a neutral rewrite removes. A probability readout can screen restatements cheaply.

source: CogBias (2026) Measuring and Mitigating Cognitive Bias in Large Language Models
finding: GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.3-70B and Qwen2.5-72B across four bias families. A 'debias' instruction helped framing but hurt financial biases.
numbers: Framing effect accuracy 35.6% biased prompt to 41.4% with debiasing (+5.8 points). Hyperbolic discounting -13.4, disposition effect -11.6. Judgment-bias shift under vanilla prompts: GPT -4.3, Llama -7.7, Qwen -2.7 points.
limits: Greedy decoding, three models, preprint; framing gains were small.
agent_relevance: A global debias instruction is a coin flip by domain. Fits our rule: change prompts only on a signal, with held-out checks.

source: CogBias (2026)
finding: Option position bias was far larger than judgment bias in the same models, and order matters for judge use.
numbers: First-option selection 77.1% to 79.0% (chance 36.8%). Order bias 30% (GPT-4o-mini), 56% (Llama), 66% (Qwen).
limits: Different metrics per family; not comparable across families.
agent_relevance: Shuffle option order in code whenever comparing framed variants, or position noise swamps frame effects.

source: More or Less Wrong (2025) A Benchmark for Directional Bias in LLM Comparative Reasoning
finding: Words like 'more', 'less' and 'equal' in a comparison question push models toward that word. Free-form chain of thought cut the push; structured JSON CoT did not.
numbers: 300 base scenarios x 14 prompt variants; 6 models (GPT-4o, 4o-mini, Sonnet 3.7, Haiku 3.5, Qwen2.5 3B and 7B). Neutral 'More' error 26% (Sonnet) to 93% (Qwen-3B). Equal cues push 'Equal' errors up to 94%. Free CoT brings most directional errors below 30%.
limits: A search summary mentioned value anchoring failing; the page I read did not, so that is not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Cue words in a question steer the answer. Restate comparisons without direction words, and let reasoning be free text.

source: DeFrame (2026) Debiasing Large Language Models Against Framing Effects
finding: Eight 3B-14B instruct models on framing-paired BBQ, DoNotAnswer and 70Decisions. Negative-framed questions produce about twice the bias. The DeFrame loop (self-revise, guideline, then answer under the opposite framing) removed most of it.
numbers: BBQ bias under negative framing 2x positive on average, up to 4x. DeFrame cut framing disparity 92% and bias score 93% on BBQ. Ablation LLaMA-3.1-8b disability bias: plain 6.984, +self-revision 1.542, +guideline 0.514, full 0.171.
limits: Fairness domain, not gain/loss choice. Its framing integration rewrites into the OPPOSITE frame, not a neutral one. Other baselines lowered harm but not the framing gap. Last third of the page not read.
agent_relevance: A working agent-loop method: answer under both frames and reconcile. Matches our S1 plus a compare step done in code.

source: Hwang et al. (2026) FRAGILE / Framing Matters: behaviorally-grounded value alignment
finding: Fact-preserving rewrites in moral, medical triage, legal and role-conflict decisions flipped Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B and Qwen2.5-7B answers far more than plain paraphrases did, for value-tinted narration and temporal slicing.
numbers: Average flip rate 28.6% over framings. Value-tinted: LLaMA 39.9%, Mistral 36.3%, Qwen 47.2% vs paraphrase 18.0%, 21.4%, 21.5%. Medical triage LLaMA 58.0%. Vividness: 17.4%, 8.6%, 14.0%, near paraphrase.
limits: Small open models only; binary choices; paraphrase flip rate (about 18% to 22%) is a floor. Vividness effects equal paraphrase noise.
agent_relevance: Include a paraphrase baseline when testing S1: report flip rate minus paraphrase flip rate. Value tint and time horizon wording matter most.

source: Hwang et al. (2026) FRAGILE
finding: Prompt-level fixes (system prompt, prefix and suffix value anchors) often made framing worse. A representation-level steering fix (VALIGN) worked.
numbers: LLaMA value-tinted flip rate 39.9% to 11.9% with VALIGN. System prompt cut flips by 7.8, 0.9 and 10.3 points (LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen); prefix or suffix anchoring on Mistral lowered stability under vividness (-5.0, -7.3).
limits: Needs hidden-state access, not usable for API models.
agent_relevance: For API agents, prefer an input-side rewrite and a check; prompt anchors alone can backfire.

source: Syntactic Framing Fragility (2026) An Audit of Robustness in LLM Ethical Decisions
finding: 23 models, 14 scenarios, four logically equivalent syntactic frames ('should X', 'should not X', 'goal even if X', 'not goal if X'). Endorsement swung strongly, especially in small open models and with negation.
numbers: Mean framing-gap index 0.53 (SD 0.27); 45.2% pairs high, 41.8% moderate, 13.0% robust. Open-source 0.79 vs US commercial 0.41 vs Chinese commercial 0.39 (H=18.7, p<0.001). Endorsement F3 vs F0: OSS 0.97 vs 0.29. 30 samples per cell, 43,680 records.
limits: The paper's own counts disagree between text and appendix (9/8/10 vs 8/7/8 models). Chain-of-thought benefit is conditional and uneven. Temperature 0.7 vs 0.0: no significant change (p=0.875, 3 models).
agent_relevance: Negation flips logic-equal prompts. Normalise negations before choosing. More samples at T>0 do not fix a frame.

source: This Treatment Works, Right? Evaluating LLM Sensitivity to Patient Question Framing in Medical QA (2026)
finding: Eight LLMs were given patient questions with positive versus negative framing of the same trial evidence. Framing lowered agreement with the evidence-based answer, and plain language did not change that.
numbers: 6,614 query pairs from 629 Cochrane reviews. Framing beta=-0.219 (SE 0.015, z=-14.72, p<0.001). Framing x style interaction not significant (beta=0.031, p=0.491). Gap often widest by turn four in multi-turn chats.
limits: Only the abstract page was read; per-model rates not available. No mitigation tested.
agent_relevance: Leading questions pull the model across turns. Re-derive the question neutrally at each turn, not only once.

source: Liu, Shang, Jin (2025) CoBRA: Programming cognitive bias in social agents
finding: A persona prompt ('Economist') did not reliably give the expected smaller Asian-disease framing effect. Only GPT-4o passed two simple checks.
numbers: 4 models (Mistral 7B, Gemma2 9B, GPT-4o Mini, DeepSeek-v3), 15 scenarios x 10 queries = 150 per condition, T=0.25, 5-point Likert. Chi-square across models p<0.01. Mistral heavily favored the positive frame; Gemma2 more neutral. DeepSeek: Economist more susceptible than Common.
limits: Likert scale, not forced choice. The tool is for programming bias via representation engineering, not a debiasing recipe.
agent_relevance: Personas are not a control for framing (matches G4: no persona voters). The Asian disease task works as a closed-loop test harness.

source: Sclar, Choi, Tsvetkov, Suhr (2024) Quantifying language models' sensitivity to spurious features in prompt design
finding: Semantically empty formatting changes in few-shot prompts moved accuracy by up to 76 points for LLaMA-2-13B. Sensitivity persists with model size, more shots and instruction tuning.
numbers: Up to 76 accuracy points spread. Format rankings correlate only weakly across models.
limits: Only the abstract page was read; tasks not listed there.
agent_relevance: Paraphrase noise is large before any framing. S1 evaluation must report a spread over formats, not one wording.

source: Deng et al. (2023) Rephrase and Respond: Let Large Language Models Ask Better Questions for Themselves
finding: Asking the model to rephrase and expand the question before answering lifted accuracy. A stronger model's rephrasing also helped a weaker model.
numbers: GPT-4 zero-shot, mean over 10 tasks 64.95% to 89.77%. Last letter (4 names) 21.36% to 86.82%; coin flip 74.55% to 99.09%; CommonsenseQA 84.09% to 85.45%. Vicuna even-month 56.19% to 60.95% with a GPT-4 rephrase.
limits: Gains came mostly from fixing ambiguity ('even month'), not bias. GPT-3.5 rephrasings sometimes added wrong constraints. Gains vary by task.
agent_relevance: An in-prompt restatement loop already works. Our plan: keep the original text, compare the model's restatement for drift in code.

source: Weston & Sukhbaatar (2023) System 2 Attention (is something you might need too)
finding: S2A has the model rewrite the context to drop opinion and irrelevant text, then answer from the rewrite. This lifted factuality and cut sycophancy.
numbers: LLaMA-2-70B-chat. Opinion-inserted TriviaQA 62.8% baseline to 80.3% S2A (oracle 82.0%, instructed prompting 71.7%). GSM-IC in-topic distractors 51.7% to 61.3%. Longform objectivity (GPT-4, of 5) 2.23 to 3.82.
limits: Costs one extra generation. Judged by GPT-4; one model.
agent_relevance: A close match to S1: regenerate the problem without leading or irrelevant content, then solve. Nearly closes the gap to the oracle (80.3 vs 82.0).

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1981) The framing of decisions and the psychology of choice (Science)
finding: Founding result, not re-opened this session: the Asian disease problem. Most people take the sure option when told lives are saved, and the gamble when told lives are lost.
numbers: As widely reported: 72% chose the sure option (200 saved) vs 28% the gamble; in the death frame 22% sure vs 78% gamble. Jones & Steinhardt Table 9 also quotes 28 and 78 for the gamble.
limits: Not opened in this run; counts from the standard literature.
agent_relevance: Baseline to compare model results against.

source: Mandel (2014) Do framing effects reveal irrational choice? (J Exp Psych: General)
finding: Human boundary: much of the Asian disease effect goes away when 'saved' is read as 'at least' or the numbers are made explicit and complementary. Part of the effect is linguistic.
numbers: Not opened; claim taken from a search summary.
limits: Unverified in this session.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as the abstract-math result in Payne 2025: explicit numbers remove the effect. Supports normalising quantifiers.

source: Cross-study synthesis by this agent (Payne 2025; Wang & Zhang 2026; Hwang 2026)
finding: Pattern across the opened papers: effects are large when frames carry extra story or missing rules, and shrink when numbers are explicit. Some large LLM framing flips are partly information differences between prompts.
numbers: Payne abstract math: no effect. Wang & Zhang: 64.5-point gap with unequal rules. FRAGILE paraphrase noise floor: 18% to 22%.
limits: Our own synthesis, not a single paper; treat as a hypothesis to test.
agent_relevance: S1 should rebuild the problem from a structured form (options, probabilities, outcomes) and render it neutrally.
